title: Paper cup or can: which one rolls off the desk? The can at 1.3 s; the cup circles, back in 5 s
description:
Paper cup or can: which one rolls off the desk? The can. Both get the same nudge, 0.3 m/s, 40 cm from the edge of a level desk. The can rolls straight and its centre passes the edge at 1.333 s. The paper cup rolls in a circle about the tip of its cone and is back where it started after 4.99 s, having turned 7.269 times; its track never comes closer than 10.9 cm to the edge.

Model: top view, real time. The cup is a thin-walled 8 oz paper cup (top diameter 8 cm, bottom 5.5 cm, height 9 cm; the wall plus a bottom disc of the same sheet) lying on its side; the can is 8 cm in diameter and 12 cm long. Both lie with their axes parallel to the edge, 40 cm from it, on a desk with grip 0.5 (chosen), g = 9.807 m/s^2. The nudge sets each centre moving at v = 0.3 m/s toward the edge. The can rolls straight without loss, leaves as its centre passes the edge and falls freely from 75 cm. The cup is a slice of a cone: slant sqrt(9^2 + 1.25^2) = 9.086 cm, half-angle alpha = asin(1.25 / 9.086) = 7.907 deg. Rolling without slipping, its contact line passes through the cone's apex, l1 = rb / sin alpha = 19.99 cm beyond the small rim and l2 = Rt / sin alpha = 29.08 cm from the large rim; both rims run on circles about the apex, so the cup turns l2 / Rt = 1 / sin alpha = 7.269 times per lap. Its centre of mass sits 24.05 cm from the apex along the axis and rides a circle of radius rho = 23.82 cm at a constant height of 3.309 cm; the axis turns at Omega = v / rho = 1.2592 rad/s, the cup spins at Omega / sin alpha = 9.1533 rad/s (1.4568 turns a second), and one lap takes 2 pi rho / v = 4.99 s. The friction needed to hold the circle is v^2 / (g rho) = 0.0385 of the weight, 13.0 times under the desk's 0.5; from dL/dt = Omega z x L the resultant of the normal force sits 24.08 cm from the apex, inside the 19.99 to 29.08 cm contact segment, so the cup does not tip. The rotation matrix is integrated by RK4 at 100 steps per frame (dt = 1.67e-04 s) for 5.2 s and compared with the closed form.

Measured:
- Can: straight off the desk 1.333 s after the nudge (1.592 turns over the 40 cm), down on the floor 0.391 s later at 1.724 s, 11.73 cm out from the edge.
- Cup: back through its start direction after 4.989821 s (closed form 4.989821 s), 7.269113 turns per lap; the large rim's circle reaches 29.08 cm toward the edge from the start line, so the nearest approach is 10.92 cm, at a quarter lap, 1.247 s after the nudge. The drawing holds the cup at its start after one lap; without loss it would circle for ever.
- Other cups and nudges: a 12 oz cup (top 9, bottom 6, height 10 cm) circles at 30.34 cm, 6.741 turns per lap, lap 5.13 s; a 4 oz cup (top 7, bottom 5, height 6 cm) circles at 21.29 cm, 6.083 turns per lap, lap 3.66 s; a straight cup (alpha 0, like the can) has its apex at infinity and rolls off at 1.333 s. Nudge 0.2 m/s: lap 7.48 s, friction needed 0.0171, the can off at 2.000 s; nudge 0.5 m/s: lap 2.99 s, friction needed 0.107, the can off at 0.800 s.
- Checks: 26 checks against the expected numbers, 0 failed; no slip at either rim within 8.6e-14 m; the centre of mass height constant to machine precision; the RK4 lap against the closed form within 9.8e-15 s; a half-step rerun moves the lap by 1.8e-15 s; the normal resultant by finite differences agrees with the closed form (spread 5.4e-13 cm).

Why: a can is straight, so both ends travel the same distance each turn and it rolls straight over the edge. A cup is a slice of a cone: its wide end travels farther each turn than its narrow end, so it curves around the point where the cone would come to a tip, and it needs only 0.0385 of its weight in grip to stay on that circle.

Deterministic, no seed. Rerun sims/cuproll/cuproll.py with projects/cuproll/manifest.json and you get these numbers exactly.
